## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

5	from_name: "Mark Levison"

11	[![Agile Pain Relief Consulting logo](https://do0ne7yeju3uz.cloudfront.net/uploads/image_upload/image/1059397/embeddable_0677c1aa-a480-4b68-910a-a151abad3ff9.png)](https://agilepainrelief.com/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=ebook&utm_content=subscribe)

17	
18	Hi {{ subscriber.first\_name }},
19	
20	Ever feel like you're drowning in a sea of Product Backlog Items (PBIs)? You're not alone. But can you imagine having over 1,000 items in your Product Backlog? 🤯
21	
22	  
23	
24	I'm not just making that number up to be dramatic. I had a conversation recently and someone told me they had "over 1,000 items in the Product Backlog, for one team". I'm not sharing that to shame them at all because, I'll confess, this is something I struggle with as well in our small team (just not to that extreme). If I was a betting person, I would put money down that most of you can relate as well.
25	
26	  
27	
28	One of the most common things we tell ourselves is that we need to put things in the backlog so we don't lose that small kernel of the "great idea" that we'll implement "some day". The Agile point of view is that —if it really is a gem— we will find it again. And the truth is, the version we wrote down a year ago would probably restrict us from finding a better solution when we revisit it.
29	
30	  
31	
32	When your backlog is massive, it's easy for your team to feel disconnected from the bigger picture, leading to a sense of futility and a lack of progress. 1000 PBIs isn't just intimating and inefficient, it's enough to make motivation and engagement plummet (not to mention blood pressure spike).
33	
34	  
35	
36	So what's the solution? Story Mapping. It's a powerful technique designed to bring order to chaos by visually organizing your User Stories. Instead of a flat, overwhelming list, Story Mapping helps you:
37	
38	  
39	
40	\- **Understand the flow**: See how users interact with your product through "User Steps" and "Activities."
41	
42	\- **Connect to the Vision**: Clearly link day-to-day work to the overall product strategy.
43	
44	\- **Identify Gaps**: Uncover missing functionalities or user journeys.
45	
46	\- **Facilitate Tradeoffs**: Provide a clear visual aid for discussions with stakeholders.
47	
48	  
49	
50	Even if your backlog isn't quite at the 1,000-item mark, Story Mapping offers a clearer, more manageable way to visualize your product's direction and ensure your team is always working on what matters most. Story Mapping isn't just about organizing tasks - it's a strategic tool that brings clarity, reduces uncertainty, and provides a visual roadmap for predictable delivery. It helps ensure you're building the \_right\_ thing, not just shipping features.
51	
52	[![Your Scrum Pain is Real - Take our Agile Checkup](https://www.dripuploads.com/uploads/image_upload/image/4617351/embeddable_ba429ae5-0085-4fe6-98b9-29559ae86e40.png)](https://agilepainrelief.com/agile-checkup)
53	
54	Story Mapping brings clarity to your Product Backlog, ensuring you're building the right thing. However, Effective Scrum is about more than just the backlog. Many teams struggle with other common challenges that hinder progress and create workplace uncertainty. If you're ready to diagnose and address your team's pain points, from scope creep to ineffective retrospectives, there's a quick way to find out where to focus and get practical solutions you can implement right away.
55	
56	  
57	
58	**Take our 5 Minute Agile Checkup:**
59	
60	[https://agilepainrelief.com/agile-checkup/](https://agilepainrelief.com/agile-checkup/)
61	
62	If your Product Backlog is a source of stress and you want to experiment and create a strategic roadmap, you can do a deeper dive here for step-by-step help: 
63	
64	[Drowning in an Oversized Product Backlog? Story Mapping Is Your Life Raft](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/drowning-in-oversized-product-backlog-story-mapping-is-your-life-raft/)
65	
66	  
67	
68	The Story Mapping approach has significantly reduced workplace uncertainty in many teams I know, and will help your team regain focus and momentum.

[![Agile Pain Relief Consulting logo](https://do0ne7yeju3uz.cloudfront.net/uploads/image_upload/image/1059397/embeddable_0677c1aa-a480-4b68-910a-a151abad3ff9.png)](https://agilepainrelief.com/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=ebook&utm_content=subscribe)

[linkedin.com/in/marklevison](https://www.linkedin.com/in/marklevison)

Hi {{ subscriber.first\_name }},

Ever feel like you're drowning in a sea of Product Backlog Items (PBIs)? You're not alone. But can you imagine having over 1,000 items in your Product Backlog? 🤯

  

I'm not just making that number up to be dramatic. I had a conversation recently and someone told me they had "over 1,000 items in the Product Backlog, for one team". I'm not sharing that to shame them at all because, I'll confess, this is something I struggle with as well in our small team (just not to that extreme). If I was a betting person, I would put money down that most of you can relate as well.

  

One of the most common things we tell ourselves is that we need to put things in the backlog so we don't lose that small kernel of the "great idea" that we'll implement "some day". The Agile point of view is that —if it really is a gem— we will find it again. And the truth is, the version we wrote down a year ago would probably restrict us from finding a better solution when we revisit it.

  

When your backlog is massive, it's easy for your team to feel disconnected from the bigger picture, leading to a sense of futility and a lack of progress. 1000 PBIs isn't just intimating and inefficient, it's enough to make motivation and engagement plummet (not to mention blood pressure spike).

  

So what's the solution? Story Mapping. It's a powerful technique designed to bring order to chaos by visually organizing your User Stories. Instead of a flat, overwhelming list, Story Mapping helps you:

  

\- **Understand the flow**: See how users interact with your product through "User Steps" and "Activities."

\- **Connect to the Vision**: Clearly link day-to-day work to the overall product strategy.

\- **Identify Gaps**: Uncover missing functionalities or user journeys.

\- **Facilitate Tradeoffs**: Provide a clear visual aid for discussions with stakeholders.

  

Even if your backlog isn't quite at the 1,000-item mark, Story Mapping offers a clearer, more manageable way to visualize your product's direction and ensure your team is always working on what matters most. Story Mapping isn't just about organizing tasks - it's a strategic tool that brings clarity, reduces uncertainty, and provides a visual roadmap for predictable delivery. It helps ensure you're building the \_right\_ thing, not just shipping features.

[![Your Scrum Pain is Real - Take our Agile Checkup](https://www.dripuploads.com/uploads/image_upload/image/4617351/embeddable_ba429ae5-0085-4fe6-98b9-29559ae86e40.png)](https://agilepainrelief.com/agile-checkup)

Story Mapping brings clarity to your Product Backlog, ensuring you're building the right thing. However, Effective Scrum is about more than just the backlog. Many teams struggle with other common challenges that hinder progress and create workplace uncertainty. If you're ready to diagnose and address your team's pain points, from scope creep to ineffective retrospectives, there's a quick way to find out where to focus and get practical solutions you can implement right away.

  

**Take our 5 Minute Agile Checkup:**

[https://agilepainrelief.com/agile-checkup/](https://agilepainrelief.com/agile-checkup/)

If your Product Backlog is a source of stress and you want to experiment and create a strategic roadmap, you can do a deeper dive here for step-by-step help: 

[Drowning in an Oversized Product Backlog? Story Mapping Is Your Life Raft](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/drowning-in-oversized-product-backlog-story-mapping-is-your-life-raft/)

  

The Story Mapping approach has significantly reduced workplace uncertainty in many teams I know, and will help your team regain focus and momentum.

  

If you already use it, or if you give it a try, please hit reply and tell me about your experiences. If you're a fan of Story Mapping, what was the turning point that convinced you? If you tried it and didn't like it, what didn't you like? I genuinely want to know and I read all replies.

  

Cheers,

  

Mark

3	description: >
4	  Deliver editing feedback on Mark's Markdown writing as inline CriticMarkup annotations,
5	  reviewed in Obsidian's Track Changes side panel. Use this skill whenever Mark asks you to
6	  edit, mark up, suggest edits on, or give feedback on a piece of writing that lives in a
7	  Markdown file -- blog posts, newsletters, emails, ebooks, social media posts, sales and
8	  marketing copy, or any other prose. Also trigger on "edit this," "mark up my draft,"
9	  "track changes," "use CriticMarkup," "suggest edits inline," "review with CriticMarkup."

13	  this skill decides HOW to deliver it.
14	---
15	
16	# CriticMarkup Editing
17	
18	When Mark asks for feedback on writing that lives in a Markdown file, deliver it as inline
19	**CriticMarkup** annotations written directly into the file. Mark reviews each suggestion in
20	Obsidian's **Track Changes** side panel and accepts or rejects it. The AI suggests; Mark
21	decides. You never rewrite his prose outside a markup wrapper.
22	
23	This is a delivery mechanism, not a rubric. The substance of the feedback still comes from
24	the relevant voice/style rubric (see "How This Composes" below). This skill defines the
25	format and the protocol.
26	
27	## The Setup (already installed)
28	
29	- Obsidian plugin: **Track Changes** (`.obsidian/plugins/track-changes/`, by Phil Baum).
30	  Reviews CriticMarkup suggestions in a side panel -- accept, reject, or reply.
31	- Adapted from the plugin's reviewer skill:
32	  https://github.com/philphilphil/obsidian-track-changes/tree/main/docs
33	- The vault is git-backed (auto-commits), so in-place edits are recoverable. Annotating the
34	  file in place is correct and expected -- do NOT write to a `-reviewed.md` copy, because
35	  that would break the in-panel review workflow.
36	
37	## The Five Markup Types
38	
39	| Type | Syntax | Use for |
40	|---|---|---|
41	| **Comment** | `{>>Claude: your note<<}` | The default. Any feedback that needs explanation -- a "why," a question, a structural observation, a voice slip. Always prefix with `Claude:`. |
42	| **Addition** | `{++text to insert++}` | Propose inserting words/sentences. |
43	| **Deletion** | `{--text to remove--}` | Propose cutting words/sentences. |
44	| **Substitution** | `{~~old text~>new text~~}` | Propose replacing a specific span. The cleanest form for a concrete reword. |
45	| **Highlight** | `{==text==}` | Draw attention to a passage without proposing a specific change (often paired with a following comment). |
46	
47	## Protocol
48	
49	1. **Read the file**, then identify what to flag using the matching voice rubric (How This
50	   Composes, below). If you can't tell which channel it is, ask once.
51	2. **Annotate in place.** Place each annotation immediately after (or wrapping) the passage
52	   it concerns, so it lands in the right spot in the side panel.
53	3. **Comment for anything that needs a "why."** Reserve `++ / -- / ~~` for edits that are
54	   self-explanatory (a clear typo, an obvious tighten, a banned word swap). When the change
55	   is a judgement call or carries reasoning, use a `{>>Claude: ...<<}` comment -- optionally
56	   alongside a substitution so Mark sees both the proposed wording and the reason.
57	   **Default to no comment.** A house-rule correction (GenAI vs bare "AI", ScrumMaster
58	   spelling, a banned buzzword, a typo) gets the bare `{~~old~>new~~}` and nothing else --
59	   Mark reads it and decides whether it makes sense. Most edits are like this. Reserve a
60	   comment for a genuine judgement call or a structural point Mark can't infer from the
61	   substitution itself.
62	4. **Never rewrite Mark's prose outside a markup wrapper.** Every change you make to the file
63	   must be wrapped in CriticMarkup. The untouched text stays byte-for-byte his. This is the
64	   line that keeps "AI suggests, human decides" intact.
65	5. **Reviewer name is `Claude`** on every comment, so Track Changes attributes the thread.
66	6. **Fact-check flags:** when a claim needs verification or a source, leave a
67	   `{>>Claude: [?] needs a source / verify this stat<<}` comment rather than guessing or
68	   inventing a citation.
69	7. **Grammar/spelling: off by default.** Focus on substance, voice, structure, and content.
70	   Only mark typos and mechanical grammar when Mark says so (e.g. "including typos," "copy
71	   edit it," "proofread"). When he does, deliver those as `++ / -- / ~~` since they're
72	   obvious fixes.
73	8. **Don't over-mark.** This is feedback, not a red-pen massacre. Prioritise the changes that
74	   matter, the way the chat-bullet versions of these skills rank "Priority Fixes." A draft
75	   with three real problems gets three annotations, not thirty.
76	9. **After annotating, post a short chat summary** -- a couple of lines on the shape of the
77	   pass (e.g. "8 suggestions: 2 structural comments, 4 substitutions, 2 cuts. Biggest one is
78	   the weak opening at the top.") so Mark knows what to expect before he opens the panel.
79	   Honour the chunked-delivery preference: lead with the overview, don't narrate every mark.
80	
81	## Reply Threading (when Mark responds in the file)
82	
83	Mark may reply to a suggestion by adding an adjacent `{>>Mark: ...<<}` comment. On a return
84	pass:
85	
86	- Threads Mark marked **done** (and you've verified the change landed): remove the resolved
87	  thread.
88	- Threads marked **ignore** or **won't fix**: leave them; don't re-litigate.
89	- Questions or counter-arguments: add a follow-up `{>>Claude: ...<<}` comment in the thread.
90	- The goal is **convergence** -- a clean document with only resolved threads left.
91	
92	## Scope: Applies to All of Mark's Markdown Writing
93	
94	Blog posts, newsletters, emails, ebooks, social media posts, **and sales/marketing copy**.
95	
96	This supersedes the older "suggest in chat only, never touch the file" rule for Mark's copy
97	(see memory `feedback-no-ai-edits-to-copy`). CriticMarkup honours the same intent -- the AI
98	proposes, Mark disposes -- it just puts the proposals inline where he can accept/reject them
99	instead of in a chat list. The hard line is unchanged: **never rewrite his prose outside a
100	markup wrapper.**
101	
102	## Fallback: Chat Bullets
103	
104	CriticMarkup needs a file. When the content is pasted into chat (not a file Mark points at),
105	fall back to the rubric's normal chat-bullet output. If Mark pastes a draft and clearly wants
106	inline marks, offer to save it to a file first.
107	
108	## How This Composes With the Voice Skills
109	
110	This skill is the HOW. These skills are the WHAT -- read the matching one to decide what to
111	flag, then deliver the findings as CriticMarkup:
112	
113	| Draft type | Rubric (WHAT to flag) |
114	|---|---|
115	| Blog post | `Skills/apr-blog-critique.md` |
116	| Newsletter / email | `Skills/apr-newsletter-reviewer.md` |
117	| LinkedIn / social post | `Skills/apr-linkedin-style.md` |
118	| Sales / marketing copy | `Skills/Marketing/copy-editing/SKILL.md` (sentence-level), `Skills/storybrand-messaging/SKILL.md` (page-level narrative) |
119	
120	Mapping rubric output to CriticMarkup:
121	- A flagged voice slip, anti-pattern, or content gap with a "why" -> `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
122	  comment at the spot, optionally with a `{~~...~>...~~}` showing the suggested fix.
123	- A "Suggested fix: [rewritten phrase]" from a rubric -> `{~~old~>new~~}` substitution.
124	- A cut -> `{--...--}`. An add -> `{++...++}`.
125	- A section-level observation (structure, missing CTA, weak opening) -> a `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
126	  comment at the relevant heading or paragraph.
127	
128	storybrand-messaging is page-level: keep its SB7 scorecard and diagnostic checks in chat,
129	but drop its per-section alternative phrasings inline as CriticMarkup at the passages they
130	concern.
131	
132	## Guardrails
133	
134	- Never edit text outside a CriticMarkup wrapper. No silent rewrites, ever.
135	- Reviewer name `Claude:` on every comment.
136	- Don't invent facts or citations -- flag with `[?]` instead.
137	- Respect Mark's hard rules inside your suggestions too: no emdash (use a spaced hyphen or
138	  `--`), never "delve," "ScrumMaster" one word, "GenAI"/"LLM" not bare "AI" for generative
139	  tools, never call LLMs intelligent.
140	- Ignore Mark's author notes (`// ...` working notes, italicised passages in sales pages and
141	  course outlines). Don't mark them up -- they aren't buyer-facing prose. See memory
142	  `feedback-italics-are-author-notes`.
143	- Don't praise compliance with rules Mark set for himself. Flag violations; stay silent on
144	  the rest.

content.text:
Short answer: one sentence, yes; a paragraph, no.

The reason to add it is that you're offering to open source it, so a reader deciding whether to raise a hand needs to picture what "it" is. Right now "mini text only CRM, to pull discussion threads from Gmail" is enough to know it exists but not enough to know if they'd want it. One concrete detail closes that gap.

The reason to keep it to one sentence: the section is "What really matters?" and the answer is *talk to more people*. The CRM is the self-aware detour, not the point. Any more than a sentence and the detour eats the message, which undercuts the whole WIP-discipline theme you just set up.

A single line that adds the "what" without derailing, in your voice:

> It reads my Gmail locally, groups messages by person, and hands me a plain text file per contact with our history and my notes. No cloud, no LLM, nothing leaves my machine.

That does three jobs: says what it does, reinforces the local/no-cloud angle you already care about, and gives would-be users enough to say "yes, send me that." Then your existing "(A rabbit hole, on top of a rabbit hole. Classic Mark.)" still lands as the punchline.

One caution: if you add the detail, it strengthens the case for a reply CTA even more, because now you've got two things worth a reply (the outreach conversation and the tool). You could fold both into one ask.

Want me to draft that CTA line so it covers both?

Happy Canada Day, I hope most of you managed to stay warm and dry. Here in Ottawa we had 118mm of rain in less than a day. We doubled the previous record for July 1. We stayed dry, but others dealing flood basements and worse.

## Too much work in progress, too little getting done
Claude told me that a number of experiments it had designed for me were unsuccessful or inconclusive. This is odd. They haven't been run. When it first suggested the experiments they seemed interesting. Problem is that they were never the most important thing to do. Worse most of them stayed hidden and I just forgot. Claude assigned them target dates, which have all passed. A few minutes ago it told me that they failed.

Claude doesn't have context. It doesn't know what other things I have going on. It has no idea how much WIP I have or anything else. It just picked random deadlines out of thin air, added them to a note and then tells me they're not successful.

At moments like these Claude feels like the worst manager ever. No sense of priority. No understanding of Work In Progress and human capacity.

Most of the experiments are worth trying. Two problems: they became commitments, and they were never visible.

We constantly remind Scrum and Kanban teams to Visualise the Work and Limit Work In Progress. Yet here I am with my friend Claude, getting caught in the same trap. How will I avoid this in the future? Visualise the experiments as part of a Kanban board that allows me to see what experiments already exist and what other commitments I have.

## What really matters?
In theory we should all be focused on delivering valuable product to a customer. Easy.

In the current business environment that has become a little more challenging. In my attempt to probe what the market wants, Claude helped me define the experiments.

There is an easier approach. Before running experiments online, I need to talk to more people.

In typical Mark fashion, rather than just do a hard thing, I wrote myself a mini text only CRM, to pull exchanges from Gmail, without relying on Claude to read your emails. So I can be reminded who I have talked to and what we talked about. (A rabbit hole, on top of a rabbit hole. Classic Mark.) If this works well, I will open source it.

I find outreach emails to be hard to write, probably because I have no idea what to ask that doesn’t sound like an awkward sales pitch. So if you get an email from me in the next few weeks that sounds like an awkward attempt to start a conversation, bear with me.

Hit reply and let me know, where you've got stuck? Committing to everything others/GenAI suggests? Too much WIP?

## Reading Rabbit Hole

Your call.<<}, I hope most of you managed to stay warm and dry. Here in Ottawa we had 118mm of rain in less than a day. We doubled the previous record for July 1. We stayed dry, but {~~others dealing flood basements and worse.~>others were dealing with flooded basements and worse.~~}

## Too much work in progress, too little getting done
Claude told me that a number of experiments it had designed for me were unsuccessful or inconclusive. This is odd. They haven't been run. When it first suggested the experiments they seemed interesting. Problem is that they were never the most important thing to do. Worse most of them stayed hidden and I just forgot. Claude assigned them target dates, which have all passed. A few minutes ago it told me that they failed.

Claude doesn't have context. It doesn't know what other things I have going on. It has no idea how much WIP I have or anything else. It just picked random deadlines out of thin air, added them to a note and then tells me they're not successful.

At moments like these Claude feels like the worst manager ever. No sense of priority. No understanding of Work In Progress and human capacity.

Most of the experiments are worth trying. Two problems: they became commitments, and they were never visible.

We constantly remind Scrum and Kanban teams to Visualise the Work and Limit Work In Progress. Yet here I am with my friend Claude, getting caught in the same trap. How will I avoid this in the future? Visualise the experiments as part of a Kanban board that allows me to see what experiments already exist and what other commitments I have.

## What really matters?
In theory we should all be focused on delivering valuable product to a customer. Easy.

In the current business environment that has become a little more challenging. In my attempt to probe what the market wants, Claude helped me define the experiments.

There is an easier approach. Before running experiments online, I need to talk to more people.

In typical Mark fashion, rather than just do a hard thing, I wrote myself a mini text only CRM, to pull exchanges from Gmail, without relying on Claude to read your emails. So I can be reminded who I have talked to and what we talked about. (A rabbit hole, on top of a rabbit hole. Classic Mark.) If this works well, I will open source it.

I find outreach emails to be hard to write, probably because I have no idea what to ask that doesn’t sound like an awkward sales pitch. So if you get an email from me in the next few weeks that sounds like an awkward attempt to start a conversation, bear with me.

Hit reply and tell me where you get stuck. Committing to everything Claude (or anyone) suggests? Too much WIP? Something else?

Mark

content.text:
Good instinct to make this durable rather than relying on memory. Here's the cleanest way.

**Don't build a separate ledger. Derive it from the newsletters themselves.**

Every issue already carries its reading links in the "Reading Rabbit Hole" / "What's Mark Reading?" section. That folder (`APR/Efforts/Newsletter/`) *is* the record of what you've mentioned. So the recap skill should, before proposing anything:

- Grep every prior newsletter file for reading-section URLs, normalize them (strip utm params, trailing slash, http/https, arxiv abs-vs-html), and build an exclusion set.
- Drop any candidate whose URL is already in that set.

Why this beats a `mentioned.json` ledger:

- **Nothing to keep in sync.** The newsletters are the source of truth; a second file just drifts.
- **It self-heals for exactly your case.** You hand-pulled these three rather than letting the skill window pick them. A ledger wouldn't know that. Grepping the drafts does, because they're sitting in the folder with the links in them.
- **It decouples from the date window.** Right now the skill keys on "since the last newsletter." The real rule you want is "not mentioned before, then fill going back as far as needed." So date becomes the *sort order*, not a hard gate: pull a candidate pool, exclude everything already mentioned, then fill to your target count reaching further back automatically.

One scope decision before I wire it in: dedup against **reading-section links only** (my default, cleanest) or against **every URL anywhere in past issues** (also catches articles you cited in the body)? I'd start with reading-section only and widen later if a repeat slips through.

This is a change to the `apr-newsletter-reading-recap` skill (plus the skill index and build log, per your maintenance rule). Want me to make it? If so, reading-section-only unless you say otherwise.

2	name: apr-newsletter-reading-recap
3	description: Build the "Mark's Reading Rabbit Hole" section for the APR newsletter — a clean, paste-ready list of what Mark read since the last issue, links included, papers and PDFs first.
4	---
5	
6	You are building the **"Mark's Reading Rabbit Hole"** section that goes in Mark's APR newsletter. The output is a short, paste-ready Markdown list of what he has read recently, each item linked to the original source with a one-line neutral description.
7	
8	This is **not** the conversational `Readwise/reader-recap` skill. That one is a coffee-style briefing for Mark himself. This one produces newsletter copy: terse, linked, reader-facing, ordered by what his subscribers will value most.
9	
10	## Hard rules
11	
12	- **Print to chat only. Never edit a newsletter file.** Output a fenced Markdown block Mark copies himself. The newsletter is his marketing copy — suggest, never write into it (see the `no-ai-edits-to-copy` rule).
13	- **Read-only against Readwise.** Never move, tag, archive, or modify any Reader document or highlight.
14	- **Neutral descriptions only.** Each one-liner says what the piece is *about*, factually. No opinions, no "I loved this," no editorializing — Mark adds his own take. Base the description on the piece's actual content/summary, never invent.
15	- **Links to the original when possible.** Use each document's `source_url`. If it is null (e.g. an uploaded PDF/EPUB with no origin), list the title in bold with no link and add `(no source link)`.
16	
17	## Readwise access
18	
19	Use the **Readwise CLI** (Mark's preference). Read `Skills/Readwise/readwise-cli/SKILL.md` for full command reference. Confirm it is installed and authenticated:
20	
21	```bash
22	readwise reader-list-documents --location archive --limit 1 --response-fields title
23	```
24	
25	If the CLI is missing or unauthenticated, follow the setup steps in the CLI reference. The Readwise MCP (`mcp__readwise__*`) is an acceptable fallback if the CLI is unavailable.
26	
27	## Step 1: Determine the time window
28	
29	Default: **since the last newsletter**. Detect the cutoff from the newsletter folder rather than guessing.

content.text:
Good, this is exactly the "talk to people" move from the newsletter. For cold-ish research outreach the rules are almost the opposite of marketing copy: short, no pitch, make it about their world, and give them the tiniest possible thing to do first. Here's a draft you can reuse, with two slots you fill per person.

**Subject (pick one):**
- Trying to learn, not sell
- Mind if I ask you one thing?
- A question about [their world]

**Body:**

> Hi [Name],
>
> [Why you, specifically - one line: "We met at the Agile meetup in May" / "I've followed your posts on X for a while" / "Jane suggested I talk to you"].
>
> I run a small Agile training and coaching practice, and right now I'm doing the unglamorous thing: talking to people instead of guessing. No pitch, I promise.
>
> One question, if you've got 30 seconds: [the single genuine question]? Just hit reply, even a sentence helps.
>
> And if you'd rather talk it through, I'd genuinely enjoy 30 minutes to hear how it actually works for you. Grab whatever time suits you here: [link].
>
> Either way, thank you.
>
> Cheers,
> Mark

**Why it's built this way:**
- **Two slots, everything else reusable.** The "why you" line is what stops it feeling like spam; a generic version reads as a blast. It's the one thing worth 20 seconds of personalization each.
- **Low-friction ask first, call as the upgrade.** Your two goals pull against each other: a reply is easy, a booked call is a commitment. Lead with the reply so nobody bounces off the calendar link, then offer the call as an easy step up. If you made the call the only option, most would do nothing.
- **"Talking to people instead of guessing" / "No pitch, I promise"** does the de-awkwarding. It names the thing they're suspicious of (a sales trap) before they can be, which is exactly what makes cold research email land.
- **Short on purpose.** Under ~90 words. The longer it gets, the more it smells like selling.

**The one thing I need from you to sharpen it:** what do you actually want to learn from these people? The "single genuine question" is the whole email, and it should be about *their* problem, not your solution. For example, if it's GenAI-and-Agile-teams:

- "What's the most frustrating part of getting your team to actually use GenAI well?"
- "Where has GenAI helped your team, and where has it quietly made things worse?"

Tell me the research focus and I'll tighten that question (and adjust the subject line to match).

That changes it for the better. These are warm contacts, not strangers, so cut the "who I am" pitch entirely and lean on the shared history instead. It gets shorter and friendlier.

**Subject (pick one):**
- A question for a past student
- Reconnecting, plus one question
- Can I ask you something? (no pitch)

**Body:**

> Hi [Name],
>
> [Warm callback - one line: "You took my CSM back in 2023" / "You've been reading the newsletter for a while now"]. It's been too long, and that's on me.
>
> I'm doing the unglamorous thing right now: talking to people instead of guessing. You're exactly the kind of person I should be learning from, so I wanted to reach out directly.
>
> One question, if you've got 30 seconds: [the single genuine question]? Just hit reply, even a sentence helps.
>
> And if you'd rather talk it through, I'd genuinely enjoy 30 minutes to hear how things are going for you. Grab whatever time suits you here: [link].
>
> Either way, it's good to be back in touch.
>
> Cheers,
> Mark

**What changed and why:**
- **Dropped the credentials line.** They know you, so explaining who you are would read as oddly formal, almost like you'd forgotten the relationship. The warm callback does that job in half the words.
- **"It's been too long, and that's on me"** acknowledges the gap honestly instead of pretending you email them every week. That candor is very you, and it disarms the "why is Mark suddenly emailing me" question.
- **Kept "talking to people instead of guessing"** and the no-pitch framing. Warm contacts still appreciate knowing you're not about to sell them a course, and it ties back to your newsletter theme.
- **Same two-tier ask.** Reply is the easy front door, the call is the upgrade. Warm audience means more will take the call, but leading with the reply still keeps the bounce rate near zero.

Still the one thing that makes or breaks it: **the single genuine question.** It should be about their world, not your offering. Give me the research focus (GenAI and Agile teams? something else?) and I'll sharpen that line and match the subject to it.

# Handoff: Client research-outreach email (phrasing)

## What the next session is for
Continue refining a reusable **research-outreach email** Mark sends to a few people a week.
This next round is **client segment only** (people who took his training and/or subscribe to the
newsletter), and should **weave in themes from his latest newsletter**. Colleague and Friend
variants are out of scope for now (drafts already exist in the prior conversation if needed later).

The immediate unfinished business: **nail the single research question** that is the heart of the
email. Everything else is drafted.

## Context you need

Mark runs Agile Pain Relief (Scrum/Kanban training + coaching, plus a grounded-skeptic take on
GenAI for business agility). He is doing customer-discovery outreach: reconnecting with past
clients to learn what the market wants **before** running online experiments. This outreach is the
literal "talk to more people" step he committed to in his newsletter.

Warm audience: all recipients know him (past students / subscribers), so the email skips any
"who I am" credentials.

### Two goals for the email (in priority order)
1. **A reply** - a one-sentence comment back (low friction, the primary win).
2. **A booked 30-minute chat** via a scheduling link (the upgrade, for those willing).

Lead with the reply ask; offer the call as an easy step up. Do not make the call the only door.

## Working artifact: the Client email draft (not saved to any file yet)

Subject options: "A question for a past student" / "Reconnecting, plus one question" /
"Can I ask you something? (no pitch)"

> Hi [Name],
>
> [Warm callback - one line: "You took my CSM back in 2023" / "You've been reading the newsletter for a while now"]. It's been too long, and that's on me.
>
> I'm doing the unglamorous thing right now: talking to people instead of guessing. You're exactly the kind of person I should be learning from, so I wanted to reach out directly.
>
> One question, if you've got 30 seconds: [THE SINGLE GENUINE QUESTION]? Just hit reply, even a sentence helps.
>
> And if you'd rather talk it through, I'd genuinely enjoy 30 minutes to hear how things are going for you. Grab whatever time suits you here: [link].
>
> Either way, it's good to be back in touch.
>
> Cheers,
> Mark

### Why it is built this way (design decisions already made)
- **Two slots, everything else reusable:** the warm-callback line (per person) and the single
  question. The callback is what stops it reading as spam.
- **"talking to people instead of guessing" + "no pitch"** disarms the sales-trap suspicion up front.
- **Two-tier ask:** reply first, call as upgrade.
- **Short on purpose** (~90 words). Length reads as selling.
- **The question must be about THEIR world, not Mark's offering.**

### The open item: the single question
Depends on Mark's research focus. Likely GenAI + Agile teams (per newsletter). Example directions:
- "What's the most frustrating part of getting your team to actually use GenAI well?"
- "Where has GenAI helped your team, and where has it quietly made things worse?"
Ask Mark to confirm the research focus, then sharpen this line and match the subject to it.

## Newsletter ideas to pull in
Source (do not duplicate - read it): `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/2026-07-08-too-much-work-in-progress-too-little-getting-done.md`

Themes worth echoing in the outreach voice:
- **"Talking to people instead of guessing"** - the newsletter frames the outreach itself; that
  phrase already lives in both places and ties them together.
- **Too much WIP / invisible commitments** - experiments that quietly became commitments; a
  candidate angle for the research question (what teams over-commit to, incl. GenAI).
- **Grounded GenAI skepticism ("glass 1/3 full")** - Mark's honest-middle stance; keep any GenAI
  question neutral and non-hype.
- **The awkward-outreach confession** - the newsletter warns subscribers they may get "an awkward
  attempt to start a conversation." Subscribers are primed for this email; the outreach can lean on
  that shared in-joke lightly.

## Mark's voice + working rules (must honor)
- No emdash (use spaced hyphen or `--`); never the word "delve".
- "GenAI"/"LLM", never bare "AI" for the tools; never call LLMs "intelligent"; no hype.
- "ScrumMaster" one word. Casual "pub with coworkers" tone; self-deprecating; reader-as-hero
  (StoryBrand): Mark is the guide who has made mistakes too.
- This is chat drafting (no file), so deliver as chat. If it becomes a Markdown file, switch to
  CriticMarkup (never rewrite his prose outside a markup wrapper).
- Ask clarifying questions before long answers; lead with an overview, then go section by section.

## Already done (background, not this session's work)
- Contacts were created in the personal CRM at `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/personal-crm/`
  (client files under `client/`). Recipients for outreach = client files, excluding anyone in
  `personal-crm/ignore-list.txt`.
- The Colleague and Friend email variants were drafted last session (regenerate from the Client
  template if needed - swap the callback line and drop the research framing for friends).

Note: recipient names/emails are PII and intentionally omitted here; they live in the CRM repo above.

## Suggested skills for the next session
- **apr-newsletter-reviewer** - best reference for Mark's authentic voice/anti-patterns (use as the
  voice rubric even though this is an email, not a newsletter).
- **storybrand-messaging** - keep the reader-as-hero framing; Mark is the guide.
- **Marketing/copy-editing** - sentence-level tightening once the question is set.
- **criticmarkup-editing** - only if the draft is moved into a Markdown file for inline review.
- Optional: read `APR/brand-voice.md` for positioning context.
